Dear Mr. Vincent:
The reports in the press quoting your radio statoment
"We're trying right now to recruit people with sbocialized
knowledge of Japan's economy -" seems to me to be one of
the most hopeful pronouncements whioh has come out of
Washington in some time.
う
To be certain that some of the leaders in the Senate and
the House do not overlook your efforts, I am writing to
some of them with whom I am in contaot, to call your state-
ment to their attention. I have often expressed myself on
the Hill to the effect that those who really kmow and under-
894.50/10-1045
stand Japan's economy should be used both in planning the
occupation policies and in the actual administration.
Vy own disillusioning experience in Government during the war
is only typical of what happened to a number of those who had
accurate information. Eired because of an unique background
of study and experience to be the chief of the Japanese Civilian
Supplies Unit of BEw (Office of Economio Warfare Analysis). I
was placed under supervisors with no Far Eastern background.
With no basis for understanding conditions in the Orient, they
persisted in attempting to evaluate conditions within Japan in
terms of U.S. standards and requirements. My information and
opinions were ignored because they were in conflict with this
theoretical approach. Various devices were resorted to in an
effort to discredit those of us with accurate knowledge of
the country and its people, and the theories were passed on
up the line. As irrefutable evidence came out bit by bit, my
2
information was proven acourate and my conolusions sound.
S
While it was gratifying it hardly indicated that my abilities
/LE
had carried their full weight in the war effort.
You and I never happened to discuss the Far East seriously in
our occasional contacts - at Lois Maolurray's wedding, in
Chungking when you were there with Henry Wallace, and on other
occasions when we met in Washington - but I hope that some day
we can have a talk.
Anymy, pore power to you in your efforts to get people who
JANS
really know their stuff on Japan.
FILED
na
R.
Sincerely yours,
-1946
Uai
Edwin P. Gbauque
Dint
Mr. John Carter Vincent, Directob
Office of Far Eastern Affairs

Dear General Hilldring:
As you know, the Congress of
Industrial Organisations is very much interested in the
policies pursued with regard to labor in ex-enemy ceustriss
now occupied by the United States. I learned reeently
that the Army has under consideration the sending of a
mission to Japen to survey the sopial and economic
situation, including trade unions, and other questions
affecting labor.
In view of the misunderstandings
and confusion which arose in connection with the measures
taken in Germany, it seens to us that some consultatiem
with the major labor organisations should be hed before
the labor policies in relation to Japan take on & pattern
hard to change.
It mmy be that this mission is net
considered to be the direct interest of labor orgmisations;
but insofar as its work liss within the sphere of our
interest, it appears that it would be advisable at least
that the personnel on such a mission should be kmom to us
and have our confidence.
Since I am not certain of the extent
to which the State Department is concerned in this matter,
I am sending a copy of this lettar to Assistant Secretary
Clayton.
Yours sincerely,
Michael Ross

promulgation on February 17, 1946, of six Imperial Ordinances and
a number of lesser Ministerial Ordinances and Proclamations. The
primary objective of these controls is to check inflation, and se
ondary objectives are the collection of food, taxes, and commodities.
as well as the creation of a mcre sound basi for the rationing of

894.5018

program as neceseery, but reservations are expressed as to the adequaey
or propriety of specific provisions, and as to the willingness and
competency of the present Shidehara Cabinet to apply and contimue
necossery coercive measures.
The more impor tant provisions of the new ordinances and procle-
mations are: an immediate freezing of all bank deposite as of
February 17; a surrender by March 7 of old currency of ten yen (later
lowered to five) denomination and above in exchange for frosen depes-

declarations of ownership of securities; and the creation of a bas
for the reimposition of a gereral rationing of foodstuffe.
is general agreement that the only molution to uncontrolled inflatn

Enclomure to despatch no. 277 of February 25, 1946, from the of
the United States Political Adviser, Tokyo, Japam, on the subjest
"Emergency Economic Controls of February 17, 1946".
OFFICE OF THE UNITED STATES POLITICAL ADVISER
Tokyo, Japan, February 25, 1946.
MEMORANDUM
SUBJECT: Emergency Economic Controls of February 17, 1946.
On February 16 the Japanese Government announced a program of
economic controls designed to check inflation, to facilitate the col-
lection of food and taxes, and to provide a basis for a reimposition
of extensive price control and rationing. The program became legally
effective a day later through the promulgation of the following ordi-
nances:
1. Imperial Ordinance No. 83, entitled "Emergency Financial Meas
ures" (Kinyu Kinkyu Sochirei), which was implemented by Finance
Ministry Crdinance No. 12 entitled "Emergency Financial Measures
Ordinance Enforcement Regulations" (Kinyu Kinkyu Sochirei hike
Kisoku), and Finance Ministry Proclamations (Kokuji) Nos. 24,
25, 26, 27, 28 and 29.
2.
Imperial Ordinance No. 84, entitled "Bank of Japan Note Deposits"
(Nippon Ginkoken Azukeirerei), which was implemented by Finance
Ministry Ordinance No. 13, entitled "Bank of Japan Note Deposits
Ordinance Enforcement Regulations" (Nippon Ginkoken Asukeirerei
Shiko Kisoku), and Finance Ministry Proclamation No. 23.
3. Imperial Ordinance No. 85, entitled "Emergency Property Survey"
(Rinii Zaisei Chosarei) which was implemented by Finance Minis-
try Ordinance No. 14, entitled "Emergency Property Survey Ordi-
nance Enforcement Regulations" (Rinji Zaisan Chosarei Shike
Khsoku).
4.
Imperial Ordinance No. 86, entitled "Emergency Food Measures"
(Shokuryo Kinkyu Sochirei), which was implemented by Agricul-
ture and Forestry Ministry Ordinance No. 10, entitled "Emer-
gency Food Measures Ordinance Enforcement Regulations"
(Shokuryo Kinkyu Sochirei Shiko Kisoku).
5.
Imperial Ordinance No. 87 entitled "Revision of Food Control Law
Enforcement Ordinance" (Shokuryo Kanriho Shikorei), which was
implemented by Agriculture and Forestry Ministry Ordinance No.
11, entitled "Revision of Food Control Law Enforcement Regula-
tions" (Shokuryo Kenriho Shiko Kisoku).
6.
Imperial Ordinance No. 88, entitled "Emergency Hidden Resources
Measures" (Intoku Busshito Kinyu Sochirei) which was implemented
by Ministry of Commerce and Industry Proclamations Nos. 33, 34
and 35.
These ordinances and proclamations are summarized as follows:
Imperial Ordinance No. 83, "Emergency Financial Measures", and its
auxiliary

=== Page 33 === (confidence 0.99)
- 2 -
auxiliary Finance Ministry Ordinancesand Proclamations, freese virtu
ally all non-governmental bank deposits in Japan as of February 17.
Additional deposits of old currency (see the following diseussion of
Ordinance No. 84) may be made to frozen accounts until March 7. De-
posits of new currency will be unrestricted. Withdrawals from re-
stricted deposits are permitted only far certain purposes, and then
only for limited amounts. The more important permissible withdrawals
are:
1. 300 yen per month per family head, plus 100 yen for each
additional family memher.
2. 1,0) yen for each war victim, providing the aggregate amount
paid to a family is not over 5,000 yen.
3. Payment of weges and salaries up to 500 yen per month per
person. Taxes normally collected at the source are not in-
cluded in the 500 yen limit.
4. Necessary business expenses for essentiab operations.
5. Medical, wedding and funeral expenses, up to 1,O00 yen.
6. Educational expenses up to 150 yen per month per student.
7. Operating expenses of community associations.
8. Campaign expenses.
9. Most varieties of national and local taxes (lurury taxes and
consumers taxes are generally excepted).
10. Emergency expenses, in amounts prescribed by the Finance Min-
ister.
In addition to the above-mentioned releases of funds, certain "ro-
stricted" withdrawals are permitted. These are transfers from one blocked
account to another and may be made for wages in excess of 500 yen per
month, bonuses, private debts outstanding as of February 17, insurance,
rents, and (subject to certain proofs and formalities) construction ex-
penses for approved projects.
Imperial Ordinance No. 84, "Bank of Japan Note Deposits", and the
accompanying Finance Ministry Ordinance and Proclamation, require the
surrender of all out standing currency between February 25 and March 7.
Such withdrawal allowances as are permitted under Imperial Ordinance No.
83 will be paid in new currency, and the remainder of the surrendered
currency placed in restricted deposit. The exchange may take place
at post offices, banks, and other financial institutions. Bank notes
of denominations under 10 yen need not be surrendered. (Note: ▲ further
decision on the part of the Government to require the surrender of 5 yen
notes was reported by Tokyo newspapers on February 22.) After March 2
old currency ceases to be legal tender. If sufficient new notes are
not available for immediate exchange, overstamped current issue bills
will be used temporarily.
Imperial Ordinances Nos. 86 and 87, together with various auxiliary
Agriculture and Forestry Ministry Ordinances, provide for the compulsory
requisition of rice and other staple grains, when quotas assigned to
individual

=== Page 34 === (confidence 0.99)
- 3 -
Collection may be made in the name of the Minister of Agrioulture 
of such foodstuffs for labor or commodities. Provision is also mde
for government control over the prices and urban rationing of comes
tibles.
Imperial Ordinance No. 85, "Emergency Property Survey" andthe
implementing Finance Ministry Ordinance require the filing of declara-
tions of ownership as of March 3 of various forms of liquid assets
and securities, although delay in reporting is permitted as late as
April 2. According to the preamble, Imperial Ordinance No. 85 is
intended to facilitate the collection of future taxes on war profits.
Imperial Crdinance No. 88, "Emergency Hidden Resources Measures"
and the auxiliary Ministry of Commerce and Industry Proclamations
provide for the filing by March 10 of a declaration of ownership of
specified types of property as of February 17. These forms of prop-
erty include virtually all categories of machinery, equipmont, raw
materials, etc., which could be of value in connection with the ro
vival of production. Transfers, concealments or alterations before
April 20 are forbidden.
Prime Minister SHIDEHARA and Chief Cabinet Secretary NARAHASHI
issued statements at the time of the announcement of the above ordi-
nances. Both justified the drastic character of the controls through
a description of the dangers of Japan's present economic crisis, and
indicated thet further measures such as price regulation, rationing.
and the stimulation of production would follow.
Press comment was extensive and varied. Unanimous approval of
the program as at least an attempt to combat inflation was coupled
with almost as general expression of doubt as to its adequacy on
numerous counts. Most newspapers regretted the government's delay
in acting, and the consensus was that the success of the program
depends upon the strict enforcement of the various ordinances, as well
as the development of sound, additional plans for increasing produo-
tion.
Only the Communist Party condemned the program outright. Other
parties, while critical of the timing and various provisions of the
enactment and suspicious of both the intentions and capacities of
the present Cabinet, appeared willing to cooperate. Specifically.
party reactions were as follows:
Progressive: Public welfare must be protected by prohibition
of barter, especially in foodstuffs, by elimina-
tion of. black market activities, and by downward
revision of the recently increased transportation
rates. But more goods must be produced to effect
any real solution, and adequate production capital
must be provided.
Liberal: Government now must clarify plans for importation of
food and for rationing. Popular cooperation is
essential, and the party pledges support.
Communist: Under the guise of curbing inflation, the measures
are new oppressions of the messes. The farmers
are hit

=== Page 35 === (confidence 0.99)
are hit by compulsory purchases of food, thew
wokkers by restrictions on wages, and mall
ness men by continued uncertainties. Meanwhil
privileged classes have already taken evasive
ures and are favored by the exemptions of the enmet
ments. Production increase--the real solution-is
still menaced by capital's refusal to renew opera-
tions.
Socialist: Provisions of the program are inadequate to lower or
stabilize prices. Fundamental evils, such as pay-
ments on government bonds and indemnification of
wartime business capital, are not faced. Only a
truly democratic government can combat inflation.
Cooperative: Immediate enforcement of war profit tax, suspension
of bond payments, and use of funds for social works
and unemployment relief are further required. An
immediate "price fixing" system must be established.
Financial circles approve of the program with reservations, although
a return to bureaucratic controls is distasteful. In the opinion of
these groups, the weak points of the government's measures are: failure
to distinguish between urban and rural residents on allowable withdrawals;
lack of adequate provision for use of business capital; and a general
lack of emphasis on increased production.
The promulgation of this control legislation produced an immodiate
reaction on business. Black market prices showed a slight initial
decline, which was followed by sharp rises as a result of "last fling"
purchases. Theaters and places of amusement were crowded. Curroney of
smaller denominations, unaffected by the currency surrender ordinance,
soon disappeared from circulation, and widespread difficulties in con-
ducting small transactions have resulted. On February 22, a decision
to require the surrender of five yen notes was announced by the govern-
ment in an effort to check hoarding. In a joint statement the Metro-
politan Police Board and the Procurator's Office indicated an inten-
tion to prosecute "acts of grudging" (withholding change) or "profit
eering" (forcing additional article on a pur chaser in lieu of change)
with requests for sentences up to three months imprisonment. ▲ possi-
ble unmanageable rush to convert currency on the final days of grace
was anticipated by banks and post offices.
T. L. Blakemore

INTERROGATION OF - TSUDA, ShUO
AT - Peiping, Oct. 25,
BY - Albert H. Mackenzie
formerly F.E.A.,now
Prescott, Arizona.
An interview with TSUDA, Shuei, V-Pres. of the KITASHINA
KK
KAIHATSU (North China Development Co.) in Peking revealed him
to be the slipperiest, most repugnant Japanese official I met
anywhere in China. His elusive ways and failure to produce re-
ports I had asked him for caused me to warn him personally that
if he did not co-operate I would be obliged to turn him over
directly to the military and see to it that the War Crimes Tri-
bunal made a special investigation of his case. This produced
some but not satisfactory compliance. I also reported his case
to the O.S.S. officers in Peking and turned in my report on him
to JICA.
For review, the information shows that he was born in Kana-
zawa. From Dec. 1943 to the end of the war he was one of the
two V-Pres. of KITASHINA KAIHATSU. The other V-Pres. was NAKA-
MURA, Kojiro. TSUDA, SAN concerned himself with the operations
and management of the KAImATSU involving also the establishment
and
of new operating companies th industries, whereas NAKAMURA
was its chief Finance Officer.
The President of KAIHATSU, from May, 1945, to the war®s end
(yoshiaki?)
was one HATTA, Kamei. For 3t years prior to this, its President
was TSUSHIMA, Juichi, who had returned to Japan to become Min-
ister of Finance.

=== Page 74 === (confidence 0.99)
As to some antecedent events in TSUDA'S career, prior to b
coming V-Pres. of the KAIHATSU, he was V-Pres. of the Mining Con-
trol Ass'n. in Japan from 1940 to December, 1943. Previous to
1940, and back to 1938, TSUDA had beon in China as manager of the
North China Gold Mining Company which, having been established in
operated and owned 25 gold mines in North China, averred TSUDA.
Frior to 1938, TSUDA had, for 22 years, been with Sumitomo
in the head office of their mining division.
Although it has been made clear previously, and in other re-
ports as well, TSUDA puts the number of affiliated operating com-
panies under the KAIHATSU at 64,with some 14 subsidiaries, not
identified, under that 64. In any case, the aforesaid 64 operat-
ing companies were classified under three categories by TSUDA as
follows:
(1) Public Utilities,
(2) Basic Industries and Mining,
(3) Temporary (Experimental) Enterprises.
He further stated that a good 51% of al1 Japanese in North
China worked with one or more of the 64 operating companies of
KAIHATSU.

=== Page 75 === (confidence 0.99)
INTERROGATION OF IZAWA, M1chio
AT Peiping, October 26, 1945
BY Albert H. Mackenzie,
formerly F.E.A., now
Prescott, Arizona
Cor was this Kamei
Interview with IZAWA, Michio, Advisor to HATTA, Yoshiaki,
an ex-Cabinet Minister and latterly President of the KITASHINA
KAIHATSU KK (North China Development Company). IZAWA was also
Chief of the CHOSA KYOKU (Research and Analysis or Investigation
Section) of the KAIHATSU. He had held this important job from
May, 1942, to the end of the war. IZAWA states that he is a
former Director of the SMU.
The most important endeavor of his Research Section was to
make continual and expanding geological surveys of North China.
It was particularly important to locete cok ing coal.70% to 80%
of that used in Japan came from North China fields, stated
IZAWA. (In my earlier reports I accepted this as true, but now
I doubt it).
Next important was iron ore for which there had been ur-
gent deposit searches in both North China and Mongolia. (IzAwA
produced two copies of his Section's Geological Survey map of
North China, one of which was sent to a language translation
section of G-2 in Shanghai).
IZAWA, obviously a very intelligent and capable man,
fore-
stated that he saw and therefore advised strongly, the neces-
sity of setting up factories in North China to build machinery,
and particularly mining machinery. en the oontinent. In due

=== Page 76 === (confidence 0.98)
time, aacordingly,-one.large-company-was-(said--he
never got to see it) completed at Tientsin, six to twelve
before the war ended. It was set up to build mining machinery.
Sumitomo experts and equipment were used.
In answer to the question how long in his opinion it would
take for the Chinese to assume full control over the KAIHATSU
and its some 64 operating companies, IZAWA stated that a Mr. Kuo
and Mr. Ku had come from Chungking nearly two months ago but
their staff was neither big enough nor well-trained enough to
take over fully yet. IzAWA could not say how big a quota of
skilled Japanese experts and technicians would be retained by
the Chinese even after the transition period, but he allowed
that the Chinese wanted a goodly number to stay on and that the
Japanese technicians themselves were quite willing to stay. Said
IZAWA: "The Chinese when they get started will find themselves
incapable of running these enterprises. Without Japanese skill
all factories will stop".
In response to the question put to every Japanese official
interviewed in North China as to what intelligence organization
or system was set up within KAIHATsU, or within any of its af-
filiates, his answer appeared to bo genuine that there was no
intelligence unit or bureau,as such,within this industrial network
but that most questions coming from the Army ar Navy would filter
down from the Develcpment Co. officials level to the Transporta-
tion Co. (KOTSU) because the latter had the greatest ramifica-
tions, number of workers and guards. In this connection, he
added further that quite recently, that is to say about October,
1944, the KERO HOMBU (Police and Labor HQ.) was established by the
KAIHATSU and small groups under it were assigned to protect various
mines and other establishments from the Pa Lo Jin. The KErRo HOMBU
C

=== Page 77 === (confidence 0.98)
was treated in addition to the elaborate protective guard
system which the railroads have. (Note:--Compare this with
the testimony given by TSUDA, V-Pres. of the KAIHATSU. Thoir
evidence tallies on the existence of the KEIRO HOMBU)
Never-
theless, its functioning seems to have been like that of all
the remaining quasi-intelligence units within the civilian or
industrial operations of North China in that it was very ir-
regular and inefficient.
IZAWA added that the KEIRO HOMBU acted as a channel for
"obvious" political information but the "delicate stuff" was
procured by Army men.
His CHOSA-KYOKU generally had about 5O men in the field
collecting geological data. He added that Mr. TSUDA was re-
sponsible for producing all information on the status of fac-
tories and plants within the KAIHATSU.
An interesting financial side light given by IZAwA was
that although the Japanese Army purchased materials and pro-
ducts at fair prices during the war years from the various
operating affiliates of the KAIHATSUx in order that its plants
could stay in existence, still, the KAIHATSU was able only to
pay the 6% which it guaranteed to stockholders by borrowing
from F.R.B. here in North China. Thence the credit of 6%
would be transferred to the Bank of Japan for the payment of
dividends to the stockholders. IZAWA is not sure but he be-
lieves that the F.R.B. ratio to Japanese yen was held at 1-to-1
(Note that this produced the fictitious picture of a steady maintenence

Remember that the KAIHATSU was a holding company. IZAWA
stated that when any of the 60-some operating companies needed
money,the KAIHATSU, or holding company, would borrow from one
of the three banks in North China, namely; the F.R.B., Bank of
Chosen, and the Y.S.B., and credit the money borrowed to the
affiliated operating company. In this manner it was felt that
the financial orerations of any affiliate com any could not get
out of hand. As above indicated, the holding company did not
conduct or operate any auxiliary banking business as such. In
addition to the process of borrowing from the aforesaid three
banks in North China it would also, on occasion, borrow in Japan
proper by floating bonds on behalf of,and secured by, the 60 oper-
ating companies. This procedure became impossible over the last
year and a half before surrender, hence the KAIHATSU was reduced
to either of the two alternatives of borrowing from F.R.B. (which
often amounted to a mere issue of new currency) or from the three
above-named Japanese banks. The total debt of the North China
Development Company at the end of the war as estimated by IZAWA
was 50 to 60 billion yuan--an indebtedness distributed in fractions
unknown to him to the F.R.B., to the Y.S.B. and to the Bank of
Chosen. IZAWA purports to have receivad this particular estimate
& debt of

China enterprise system).

AT - Peiping, Oet. 25,1
BY - Albert H. Mackenzio

MITSUYUKI, Hisahi, was interrogated in Peking. He had beon
Chief of the Propaganda and Publicity Section of the KITAsHINA
KOTSU KK (North China Transportation Company) an affiliate oper-
ating company of the KAIHATSU. The averred function of his Section

Upon being questioned concerning any intelligence activities

that practically all requests from the Army or Navy or from Tokyo
came to them through the Embassy in Peking (see the interrogation
on Lt. Gen. KUSUMOTo) except upon infrequent occasions through

it

all came through the Investiga-

INTRODUCTION
This is the first issue of a bulletin of statistics relating to important
ecanomic activities in Japan. Data bave been obtained for the most part from
Japanese sources - primrily from control associations, government ministries, and
the Bank of Japan. The Matural Resources Section has furmished statistics for the
industries under its jurisdiction.
The Research and Statistics Division of the Economic and Scientific Section
is engaged in efforts to bring together into a aingle bulletin continuing series of
the more important statistics relating to the Japanese econamy. Additional series,
therefore, will be included as rapidly as conditions permit. Although the statistics
included in this bulletin appear to be substantially orrect on the basis of prelim-
inary investigations, revisions will be incorporated from tim to tim as neoessary.
Improvements in the manner in which date are obtained at the source and modificstions
directed toward more comprahensive and more detailed reporting are the first
objectives to wtich most attention is currently baing devoted.

=== Page 151 === (confidence 0.96)
DEPARTMENT OF STATE
imomic Rehabihlali
THE LEGAL ADVISER
February 261947
Le - Mr. Fahy
Le/P - itr. Snow
Subject: SWNCC paper on US policy with respect to excessive
concentration of economic power in Japan
In accordance with my discussion with General Snow of February 18,
1947, I have gone over the above-mentioned paper as carefully as time
permitted. I have also discussed the paper briefly with Mr. Martin,
894.50/2-2647
Acting Director of ESP and Mr. Vernon of IR. I have also discussed
the relevant portions of the German decartelization law with
Mr. Karasik of GA. As a result of these discussions and my examina-
tion of the relevant documents, I should like to make the following
reconmendations and to suggest that they be discussed with Mr. Martin
and Mr. Vernon as the basis upon which Le would be willing to approve
the proposed paper.
1. The recommendations made herein are based on the major
premise that Le is reviewing this paper for its legal aspects, rather
than attempting to pass on the policy of breaking up of excessive
concentration of economic power or the stringency of application of
that policy. I have not examined the background report submitted
by Mr. Corvin Edwards and have accepted the premise of the paper
that the Zaibatsu have exercised a pernicious and militaristic effect
on Japanese life, etc.
2. I believe that the paper should contain an introductory
statement with respect to the role played in the Japanese economy by
the Zaibatsu. While such a recital will not in itself justify
FILED
C
measures which would otherwise be unjustifiable, it will more
clearly outline what I understand to be the fundamental basis of the
paper, namely, that the Zaibatsu have exercised a pernicious role
in the Japanese economy, that the militaristic effects of their
influence are provable and that their economic power in Japan, com-
bined with their social and political prestige, makes them exceedingly
73
dangerous from the point of view of security. Such a preamble will
recite reasons for the drastic steps of the paper which I understand
2
to be its real basis, will give to the paper more of the character
S
of a one-time purge for reasons of security which it is supposed to
have and will, while stating some justification for the proposed
4
steps, also differentiate the program outlined in the paper from what
H
have become more the common state action of nationalization of private
property. Basing the progran on these considerations, with emphasis

=== Page 152 === (confidence 0.99)
-2-
on security necessities, will tend to prevent citation of this case
in other situations involving state action with respect to private
property.
In this connection, and as a factor which has limited these
suggestions, it may be pointed out that the basic policies which the
subject paper carries out have already been established in the Basio
Occupation Directives.
3. I suggest that the last paragraph of Section I - Objective be
amended to indicate that the measures involved are to be effectuated
by the Japanese Government. The United States cannot escape putting
forward its views on this subject for the guidance of SCAP. Never-
theless the responsibility for putting this program into effect should
be placed on the Japanese Government, acting though it may during
the present period at the direction of SCAP. The question whether
the compensation provisions of the document are in fact adequate
will thus be made less important, since the steps recommended by
the paper can then be brought within the scope of the doctrine that
ground does not lie under international law for complaint about
actions taken by a government affecting the property or interests
of its owm nationals.
4. As a corollary to the above proposition, the fact should be
explicitly stated that adequate, prompt and effective compensation
should be given, to the extent that property is taken, to United
Nations and neutral nationals. Paragraph 21 of the present document
does specify, in general terms, that SCAP shall protect the interests
of nationals of members of the United Nations in Japan; but I per-
ceive no reason why the interests of neutral nationals should not
also be protected, and it seems to me that a great deal of difficulty
would be removed if there were some.spelling out of what is meant by
such "protection". On the one hand, there is the undoubted fact
that exercise of the police power of the state does not necessarily
involve the granting of any compensation. Thus the enactment of the
Sherman Act presumably did not involve the utaking" of property by
the United States and no compensation was given for compliance with
its terms. Moreover, the program involved, by and large, does not
involve destruction of the interests of persons owming property or
businesses in Japan, but dispersal of the various units of such
businesses. In other words, a stockholder in a holding company may
find that the holding company has disappeared and that as a result
he has been given shares in the operating subsidiaries. (Cf. the
Public Utilities Holding Company Act) Compensation would not nec-
essarily be involved in such cases. Where, however, there is an
actual taking of an interest of a non-enemy national, the require-
ment of adequate, prompt and effective compensation should be
stated.

=== Page 153 === (confidence 0.99)
一3-
5. Some rephrasing of the definition of an "excessive concentra-
tion" should be made. I would suggest, for example, that the phrase
"large proportion" should be changed to "larger proportion". I feel,
however, that re-definition in this field is extremely difficult,
that our own Sherman Act testifies to the difficulties in matters of
this sort, and that the scope of the definition and the consequent
mumber of companies to be included is a matter for policy determina-
tion rather than a legal issue.
The difficulties of definition were encountered also in the
German decartelization law, and may perhaps be partially eliminated
by use of the device - used in the German case - of providing in the
law itself a list of companies affected. The list of "restricted
companies" already (as I understand it) promulgated by SCAP might be
appended for this purpose.
6. I feel that restrictlon of persons to officers and director-
ships only in the company in which they are principally engaged and
as specified in paragraph 4, is a somewhat drastic measure. It may
be necessary, as a matter of policy, under the peculiar circumstances
of Japanese feudal-industrialism. Acknowledging the influence which
has been exerted through multiplicity of directorships, etc. and the
difficulty of precise definition in such a way as to separate the
innocuous from the harmful cases, I nevertheless would suggest con-
sideration for the proposition that the policy stated in paragraph 4(c)
should be limited to a ten-year period, and that the prohibition
should be reconsidered at the end of that period.
7. I would suggest amendment of paragraph 5(c) in such a manner
as to prohibit the personnel involved only from acquiring positions
of business responsibility in any enterprises wnich have been defined
as parts of excessive concentration for the ten-year period involved,
plus the prohibition on positions of governmental responsibility
during the ten-year period. In the alternative, a clause could be
included providing for exceptions to the prohibitions stated in
paragraph 5(c) for cases in which the Zaibatsu individual does not
have funds from which living allowance will be paid during the ten-
year period. This might well also require modification of paragraph
5(b). Paragraph 5(a) might be redrafted so that divestment would be
only of corporate security holdings and business properties related
to enterprises found to be parts of excessive concentration, or
capable of being utilized to reinstate excessive concentration. So
far as divestment of liquid assets is concerned, it seems to me that
the objective of preventing these persons from buying back positions
of prestige and responsibility would be as well served by blocking
their liquid assets, plus such compensation as they receive under the
program as by divesting them of these liquid assets. Blocking could
include provision for payment of living expenses over a period of
time, plus release of the blocking at some future date when the anti-
Zaibatsu progran has been so far carried forward as to make release
of these sums, subject to the other restrictions, harmless.

=== Page 154 === (confidence 0.99)
8. I would further suggest revision of paragraph 5 in such
as to indicate that persons who may be acting on behalf of the p
sonnel described should be subjected to the same measures as are
such personnel themselves. The revised section might then go ont
state that close ties of relationship or past personal relationship
should be considered in deciding whether a person is or has been or
is likely to act on behalf of the individuals described. Such a re-
phrasing would remove a good deal of the present bill of attainder
flabor of paragraph 5.
9. I would suggest overall revision of paragraph 6 on compensa-
tion in such a way as would indicate the following:
a. To state clearly rather than by implication that the
measures specified in the paper are not applicable to non-
Zaibatsu individuals - in other words, that ordinary Japanese
nationals will not be subjected to the special measures of the
paper.
b. In many cases compensation will not be necessary at all,
since persons will merely be acquiring shares of operating com-
panies in substitution for shares of holding companies.
c. Where interests of non-Japanese nationals are effected
in some way other than by mere exercise of normal police power
of the state and in such manner that compensation would ordi-
narily be the rule of international law, compensation should be
made in an adequate and effective manner.
d. So far as interests of the Zaibatsu Japanese nationals
are concerned, where those interests are taken under the program
in such a manner that compensation would ordinarily be the rule,
compensation whould be made, but such compensation should be
blocked by the Japanese Government and for a period of ten years
such compensation or interest on it should be paid to the nationals
involved only in amounts sufficient to provide adequately for
living expenses. (This restriction should also be limited to
individuals of the sort against which the policies of the paper
are directed; minor Japanese stockholders in Zaibatsu enterprises
will under the paper be compensated fully, subject to the special
tax or increase in value since August 1945. ) Moreover, use of
the funds in question at the end of the ten-year period may be
restricted in such a way as to prevent reinvestment in industries
or enterprises which have been the subject of the program mentioned
in the paper. This would leave an ample scope for investment,
but at the same time would prevent the persons in question from
reinvesting in a way which would be likely to reinstate the evils
against which the paper is directed.

=== Page 155 === (confidence 0.99)
e. On the basis of the above, some re-examination of the
tax program suggested might well be made. I would personally
have no objection to something in the nature of an exmess profit
tax on inflation since August 1945. On the other hand, tams
specifically directed at the compensation received seems to me
to be rather undesirable. Such overall capital levy as may be
contemplated in any plan for financial reform in Japan might well
handle this problem. However, this seems a policy rather than
a legal problem.
10. The language of paragraph 6(e) seems to me to be undesirable.
I would suggest the entire elimination of this paragraph. The
measures stated above should be sufficient to prevent a resumption
of Zaibatsu power and a vague demand that other measures not defined
and not related to any standards be taken if the sums involved are
too large would seem to me to be quite unnecessary and undesirable.
A provision for re-examination of the Zaibatsu program at the end of
ten years, and the taking by the Japanese of such further measures
as may be necessary to carry it out might be substituted.
1l. I also have some question as to the necessity of requiring
succession by the owner's heirs before the freese is terminated,
but understand that tnis technique is in line with customary Japanese
practice. In any case, many of the persons involved must be of
moderately advanced age at the present time, and since longevity
is probably not being fostered by the present situation in Japan.
12. The question of protection for United Nations interests as
provided in paragraph 21 has already been treated above.
These suggestions would clearly not be sufficient if the paper
dealt with any situation other than that of Japan. It has been kept
in mind, in preparing this memorandum, that the fundamental policy
is set forth in the basic directives, so that the paper is merely
by way of implementation; that the pervasive influence of the Zaibatsu
in the Japanese economy is extraordinary, and its eradication there-
fore needs extraordinary measures; and that the steps proposed are
for a Japanese Government to impose on its own nationals, of a class
whose influence has been both great and insidious, and shows signs
of great vitality.
If amendment along the above lines is thought to justify clearance of
the proposed paper by Le, I would suggest discussion of these points
with Messrs. Wartin and Vernon, with a view toward redrafting in
accordance with these suggestions.
Seymour J. Rubin

TO
: A-H - General Hilldring
DATE: March 12, 1947
FROM : JK - Mr. Martin
suject: A Positive Economic Program for Japan.
I am enclosing three documents:
1.
The report of the Japanese Reparations Policy Committee
appointed by you and Assistant Secretary Thorp on January 15
2.
An outline of an export-import program for Japan for the
calendar years 1948-50 designed to make Japan self-sustaining
894.50/3-1247
in the latter year (and including a more tentative projection
for 1952).
2.
An economic program for Japan integrating conclusions of the
two previous documents and taking account of other related
considerations.
The economic program for Japan proposes steps designed to accomplish
the following purposes:
1. To eliminate United States expenditures in support of the Japau
economy as soon as possible and facilitate Japanese repayment of those
expenditures.
2. To create a viable Japanese economy such as would be conductive
to the emergence of a peaceful and democratic Japan.
3. To permit a substantial Japanese contribution to the economic
recovery of the Far East, which is desperately in need of the products of
CSJC
Japanese industry.
These purposes must be accomplished in cooperation with our Allies
and in such a way as to avoid charges that the United States is building
up Japan, either as a buffer against the Soviets, or as a replacement for
a currently disorganized China as our principal friend and customer in
the Far East.
The course of action proposed for accomplishing these purposes is
as follows:
SS
1. Future Japanese Imports. Food and raw material imports in excess of
disease and unrest requirements should be provided in 1948 and 1949 on
the scale necessary to "crank up" the Japanese economy within the limit
5
RM/R
of world food and commodity shortages. The cost of these additional
TE
imports should be met:
nal
(a) By
SECR
State Dep?
Econ Affois Divisi
Martin

=== Page 171 === (confidence 0.99)
SECREI
-2
(a) By active promotion of barter arrangements or short-term
financing of Japanese imports to be used to produce goods for
export, a portion of which would be assigned to pay for the
necessary imports. These arrangements should be encouraged parti-
cularly with countries which do not require repayment in dollars.
(b) To the extent that credit from private sources is not available
for the purpose described above, the liquid assets available to
SCAP in Japan should be converted into a revolving trust fund to
finance such transactions, and if necessary RFC and Export-Import
Bank financing should be sought.
(c) Japanese liquid resouroes should also be considered available
to pay for imports such as food, which cannot be incorporated in
the self-liquidating program.
2. Future Japanese Exports. The proceeds of future Japanese exports
and their contribution to the revival of the Japanese economy should be
maximized by the following steps:
(a) SCAP should, with the aid of the Allied Trade Representative
in Japan develop a detailed export-import and production plan under
wich Japan might use the increased imports to be made available
during 1948 and 1949 to achieve self-sufficiency by 1950, assuming
no reparations removals beyond Interim levels and restrictions on

A Positive Economic Program for Japan
I. Central Problem: Japanese Recovery
1. Need for Recovery. The major objectives of this country's
Japanese economic policy are:
(a) To eliminate U.S. expenditures in support of the Japanese
Economy as soon as possible, and facilitate Japanese repayment
of those expenditures.
(b) To create a viable Japanese economy, such as would be
conducive to the emergence of a peaceful and democratic Japan.
(c) To permit a substantial Japanese contribution to the
economic recovery of the Far East, which is desperately in
need of the products of Japanese industry.
Realization of these objectives patently demands an increase in
Japan's production, such as will bring into being a favorable Japanese
balance of trade, without too harsh restrictions on Japanese domestic
consumption.
This must be accomplished in cooperation with our Allies and in
such a way as to avoid charges that the United States is building up
Japan, either as a buffer against the Soviets or as a replacement for
a currently disorganized China as our principal friend and customer
in the Far East.
2. Means of Recovery. Such an increase in Japanese production
cannot be achieved until the productivity of Japanese workers and
factories has been restored through the import of food and raw materials
substantially in excess of those required for disease and unrest purposes.
It has been estimated by the Research Sub-Committee of the Japanese
Reparations Policy Committee that, if certain specified and available
increased food and conmodity imports were provided in 1948 and 1949, Japan
could be "cranked up" to the point where she might be self-supporting
in 1950 and might achieve a trade surplus thereafter. Failing such
increased imports, there appears to be no immediate prospect of a sub-
stantial expansion in Japanese production such as might render that
country self-supporting. On the contrary, the Japanese economy will
continue to deteriorate due to the cumulative effects of food shortages
and to the exhaustion of domestic raw material stockpiles.
3. Cost

3. Gost of Reggyary. It has been estimated that imereased 1948
and 1949 importe would so stimulate Japanese exporte during these yeers
that the Japasese 1948-9 trade deficits would mot be greater if "erank-
ing up" importe were provided than if only disease and unrest imperts
were provided. Although the gross cost of the proposed imports weald
exoeed that of disease and unrest" imports by more than half a billiom
dollars during each of these two years, the increased exports mede
possible by these imports will be at least as large. The data attecked
in memorandum no. 2 gives an even more favorable picture, but it is
considered wise to discount this statistical caloulation to take aceeumt
of unfavorable problems sure to arpive such as lack of balance in the
expansion of output, difficulties in controlling Jap consumption, ete.
It will be necessary, however, to have $300-500 million over and above
proceeds of Jap exports available in the first six months of calender
year 1948 to prime the pump. Something like 8150 million should be
available from the War Department appropriation, some $200 milliom from
Jap liquid resources, and $l00 million from private financial sourees.
4. Availability of Food and Raw Materiala. The present proposal
does not envisage an all-out effort to revive the Japanese economy wm-
til early in the calendar year 1948. On the basis of information our-
rently available from SCap the food necessary to provide efficient
employees for Japanese industry on a substantially expanded basis will
not be available until after the 1947 crop. It is hoped that certain
other scarce materials, perticularly coal, will be in more ample supply
by that time. It is also necessary to do a substantial job of organisa-
tion, both within Japan and intermationally, and to rehabilitate oertaim
industries such as coal miming, and certain types of facilities before
greatly expanded import of raw materials can be processed. This does mot
mean that we delay doing what we can meanwhile with other food, other raw
materials and funds on which, within the limits of our overall foreign
policy, we can lay our hands.
5. Potential Opposition to Recovery. Any program for Japanese
economic recovery will require the full economic cooperation of the Far
Eastern nations to which Japanese exports must be sold, and from whish
her imports must come. It will also require their political cooperation,
since it will call for major FEC policy changes. Most of these countries,
however, are emotionally opposed to and fearful of attempts to revive the
Japanese economy. Some substantial inducement will be necessary if their
cooperation is to be secured.
II. Auxiliary Probleme.
6. In devising a program for Japanese recovery, consideration
should be given to three muxiliary problems:
(a) The fact that the world shortage of dollars will make
it difficult for even a fully recovered Japam to repey U.S.
occupation costs in other than small amnual amounts.
(b) The fact

(b) The fact that a reparations settlememt limited to
capital removals will prove unsatisfactory from the stand-
point of the claimamts.
(c) The fact that, at present, neither SCAP mor the
Japanese government is assuming and successfully discharg-
ing gemeral responsibility for carrying out measures es-
sential to Japan's eoomomic revival.
7. U.ß Repayment. The United States wante to be repaid the
full amount of its advances for the Japamese civiliam supply progrem.
Payment can only be made in goods or dollars. The amounts are large,
the world shortage of dollars is and promises to contimme to be sombe,
and the market in the U.S. for Japanese goods is narrow. Even when
Japan becomes self-sufficient the payment problem will be acute.
3. Jepanese Reparationg. The present U.S. reparations policy
does not promise to do the claimant countries much good. Most of
them are in such a disorganised state economically that their ability
to assimilate quantities of complicated capital equipmemt into their
industrial structure is very limited, particularly equipment likely to
be in as bad condition as most of that in Japan seems to be. Im feet,
it is considered unlikely that any large portion of even the interis
program will be moved by the claimant countries. What these countries
need most are efficient and specific types of goods such as rails,
locomotives, coastal steamers, and power plants - produced to specifi-
cations, delivered soon, and without further drain on the claimants'
foreign exchange resources.
2. Effective Organisstion of Revival. At present the economio
and financial ministries of the Japanese government are weak, don't
sympathise with out program, even when they understand it, and have
little popular support. SCAP has been slow to take a positive stand
on major economic questions. To carry out a positive program for
economic revival either the Japanese Government must be reorganised into
an effective and cooperative instrument with popular support, or SCaP
must modify his present position vis-a-vis the Japanese Govermment and
be prepared to step in and make decisions on economic polioy questions.
He must also be prepared to see that they are carried out by the is-
suance of directives, where mecessary, and by a more vigorous use of in-
spection devices to prevent sabotage of economic measures. without such
a firmingip of the location of power and responsibility the odds against
the success of a revival program, great enough in any case, will be
prohibitive. It may be necessary in order to reassure private sources
of funds to set up a civilian control of economic polioy in Japan, under
SCAP but not under the Chief of Staff.

TO
Mr. Edwin M. Martin, ESP
DATE: 13 May 1947
FROM : R. W. Barnett, JK
SUBJECT:
Promotion and Control of Japanese Economic Recovery
1. Throughout the period during which the proposed State Department
policy with respect to the Promotion and Control of Japanese Eeonomie
Recovery has been under study, it has been assumed that its primary
significance lay in its recommendation for dealing with an economic
problem involved in occupation of Japen. Within the immediate time
context, that assumption is correct. Within a time context embracing
the 1900 to 194l period and projected into the next quarter century,
that assumption is fallacious. Viewed in the wider time framework, the
proposed policy contains implications reaching far beyond Japan and its
occupation period. In actuality it produces a fundamental reshaping,
8
if not reversal, of the entire economic and strategic orientation of
6
those relationships in Asia which the United States has developed over
the pis: 50 years. This fact should be frankly acknowledged. States-
manship requires a deliberated political judgment that such a reoriente-
tion will add to the honor and produce enduring advantage to the
American people as a whole.
2. Peace, economic and political stability, and improved welfare
15-1347
in Asia, not territorial aggrandizement or economic monopoly and domina-
tion, have been the historic and fundamental aims of United States
foreign policy in the Far East. American initiative in accelerating
Japanese economic recovery may be a necessary means of contributing, at
this juncture, to those ends. However, ill-conceived methods in asserting
that initiative could produce, amongst our Allies, lasting grievances
against the United States which could, in the long term, create practical
and psychological disadvantages far outweighing the advantages accruing
from wholly successful execution of the contemplated policy.
3. In the Pacific Area, where the United States enjoys overwhelm-
ing naval, air, military and administrative predominance, both actually
and potentially, serious or immediate strategic threats to really vital
United States interests do not exist. Force or the threat of force
implied in any sort of urgent unilateral action overrides or ignores,
when it is unnecessary to do so, the legitimate views and interests of
our Far Eastern Allies. Since a margin of strategic safety exists, the
United States should, in considering an important foreign policy proposal
known to affect vitally all of the countries in the Far East, exhaust all
possibility of achieving maximum international agreement to it. The FEC
is a forum in which agreement on the matter of Japan's econonic position
in the Far East can and should be accomplished.
4. The program for Promotion and Control of Japanese Economic Re-
covery should not be set in motion unless formally agreed to, after due

=== Page 201 === (confidence 0.99)
deliberation, by most, if not all, of the countriss represented on
the FEC. If gemuine support by most of the Far Eastern Commission
countries cannot be secured to the program for Promotion and Control
of Japanese Economic Recovery, I strongly recommend that that program
be redefined in the following terms:
a. A revolving fund made up initially of convertible assets in
Japan of clearly established Japanese ownership and subsequently added
to by convertible assets kmowm to have been looted but unidentified,
should be established at the earliest possible time. The part of the
fund comprising convertible assets of Japanese owmership should be put
in operation, through issuance of an interim directive, immediately
after the Far Eastern Commission has demonstrated that Commission
action on this matter will be delayed beyond June 16. SCAP authorisa-
tion to add to the fund values of unidentified loot should amit formal
Far Eastern Commission policy action.
b. The revolving fund should be limited in its use to strictly
short and medium term credit operations of a modified link character
designed to stimulate Japanese industrial productivity until the end
of 1947.
c. From January 1, 1948, until such time as an exact appraisal
may be made of the adequacy of Japanese food resources available from
domestic production, import with Congressional appropriations, and im-
port by payment of foreign exchange received from normal export proceeds,
the revolving fund should be limited in its use to projects of a self-
liquidating character, defined, however, in terms broader than mere
link operations.
d. At such time during 1948 when a correct appraisal of the rela-
tionship of Japan's anticipated food resources to the rising line of
general economic productivity can be correctly appraised, the U.S.
Government should study the problem of whether its own interests are
better served by (1) utilisation of operating capital resources still
liquid within the revolving fund for purposes of current consumption
in Japan or (2) utilisation of liquid funds in the revolving fund for
repayment of occupation costs which have accrued to that time.
e. Having made the decision called for in d., the U.S. Government
should withdraw from all responsibility for the viability of the Japan-
ese economy.
The above program might entail running a definite and kmown risk
of losing a considerable proportion of U.S. investment in accrued
occupation costs. It would eliminate from U.S. thinking the hope
(which I consider wishful) and the promise (which I consider frmudulent)
of repayment of occupation costs as a whole or future deliveries of
reparations out of current output. This program would fulfill the
Allied obligation which the U.S. Government is most sensitively amare
of, to assist the Japanese in establishing an operating peace economy,
-2

=== Page 202 === (confidence 0.99)
without repudiating the principle (contained in SWNCC 52/7) that the
problem of Japan's postmar economic readjustment is one which the
Japanese themselves must solve.
5. I submit, herewith, some fuller observations to support the
above conclusions.
-3

=== Page 203 === (confidence 0.99)
Some Opeervetione
Beimarding Pronotion and Control of Japanese Economic Recovery
1. Generel View
The proposed State Department policy position with respect to
the Promotion and Control of Japanese Eccnomic Recovery is, I believe,
brilliantly conceived in purpose and well integrated in plan. Considered
at face value and on the broad lines in which it is drawn, the policy can
probably produce no other initial reaction than one of gratification that
the U.S. Government is now preparing to take a lead in supporting a com-
prehensive program which should effect
a. revival of the latent productivity of the Japanese economy
so that Japan can support herself,
b. repayment of the costs of occupation which have been borne
by the U.S. people during Japan's post-surrender transition from
its war to a peacefully inclined economy and
c. in due course, reparations out of current output to our
war devastated Allies for damages they suffered at the hands of the
Jepanese.
Taken at face value, this plan appears to suffer only one
serious defect. Our war ravaged Allies desire immediate, not future,
compensation from Japan for the haroc Japanese hostilities and occupe-
tion have wrought in the economic and political experience of their
peoples. However, even this defect might be considered unimportant by
the United States, if it be recognized that the reparations removed
today, in whatever form, almost surely move, in several important cases,
into the hands of unpopular governments, for the present comparatively
unconcerned in the welfare objectives of their peoples. Effective con-
duct of civil wer or the repression of popular unrest appeer to be the
primary objectives of these governments. By 1950-51, this state of
affairs may have been improved, thus increasing the possibility that
reparations can at that time contribute to the strengthening of more
genuinely progressive forces in Asia, contribute to the expansion of
productivity and real economic welfare and, indirectly, contribute to
the long term political interest of the U.S. in a peaceful and prosper-
ous Far East.
2. Prerequisites for Execution of the Program
A distinction should be drawn, however, between the broad con-
cept and purposes which embrace the Promotion and Control of Japanese
Economic Recovery and the prospect for effective execution of that
policy. There are three prerequisites for its success:
a. Adequate raw materials must become available for import

=== Page 204 === (confidence 0.99)
into Japan from sources other than the U.S., obtainable on an
orderly copimercial basis, or on reasonable credit bases,
b. Adequate control of production and consumption practices
within Japan must be assured.
c. Adequate control over, or the responsible good faith of,
the Japanese Government in the post-peace treaty period must be
a certainty.
Unless these can be fulfilled there is no possibility that the
program for Promotion and Control of Japanese Economic Recovery will
accomplish repayment of occupation costs, or, through its reparations
provisons, further compensation of the claims against Japan of our war
devastated Allies beyond those met by the industrial removals program.
3. A survey of political forces stirring in Asia as a whole offers
little assurance that the three prerequisites can be met.
A. Prospects for Orderly Planning of Imports and Exporte
The program for Promotion and Control of Japanese Economic
Recovery is posited upon the assumption that raw materials will be
available for export to Japan from China, French Indo-China, Indonesia,
the Philippines, India and Korea, as well as from the U.S. Only in the
U.S. can planning of exports be done with fair prospect that commitments
made today will be made good two, four, or six months hence. The Far
Eastern countries mentioned above suffer such profound political unoer-
tainty and economic dislocation that business commitments, either by
governments or by private concerns, can be little more than commitments
to dispose of what is actually on hend or expressions of the theoretical
possibility of future sale or purchase. Motive or business desire in
this connection is irrelevant since the practical economic environment
of disrupted transport, declining productivity, runamy currency infla-
or currency control, corrupt or incompetent administrative personnel in
government and business, usually renders meaningless either plens or
commitments which call for movement of large volumes of either imports
or exports. Economic recovery or "cranking up" recuires early movement
of large volumes of both imports and exports, between Japan and these
Far Eastern countries.
B. Prospects for Production and Consumption Controls within Japan
The Control of Japanese Economic Recovery implies the need for
imposing upon the Japanese economic system a plan and an authority over
both Japanese production and Japanese consumption.
Direct Intervention
The deficiencies of Japan's successive post-surrender governments
-2

=== Page 205 === (confidence 0.99)
and the likelihood of similarly weak governments in future is recognised
by the program in the suggestion that where the Japanese Govermment fails
to act, the Supreme Commander should intervene directly to accomplish
onds desired. This is a power SCaP has always had. Despite the faet
that Japanese coal production, fertiliser production, food collections,
etc., have fallen far short both of reasonable expectation and the
urgent necessities of the Japanese situation, SCAp has shown no disposi-
tion for "direct intervention." SCAp's failure to take direct action
can be considered a consequence of his excessive confidence in conserve-
tive Japanese leadership, his natural fear of assuming, with his limited
forces, administrative or police responsibility, and SCAP's simple lack
of the technical competence in his beadquarters to do the job efficiently,
flexibly and with real authority. It is improbable that either SCap or
his successors will suddenly acquire the talent and competence to inter-
vene, in future, wisely and effectively.
Consumption Controls: Lack of Popular Support
Nevertheless, it may not be unrealistic to expect that, even
without "intervention," substantial stimulation of production may be
accomplished and, given the raw materials, its total volume vastly
increased. The Japanese, individually and collectively, have that
capacity and may be expected to exercise it. However, it appears wholly
unrealistic to hope that success on the production side automatically will
be accompanied by continued or effective curtailment of Japanese domestic
consumption, and only by continued curtailment of Japanese domestie con-
sumption can the required export surpluses be created. Japan's compara-
tively effective, though far from perfect, wartime consumption controls
were imposed by a compact militarized government which had a definite
and popularly understood objective. The objective,: winning acmajor war,
had wide popular appeal, initially under the influence of kmown military
successes and subsequently under the influence of an increasing sense of
national desperation; and to the appeal of patriotism wmas added ruthless
police coercion. Unfortunately, the reasons now offered the Japanese
people for restriction of consumption -- "fulfillment of Japan's obli-
gations to its former war victims" -- cannot have the same popular
appeal; nor can that slogan be enforced through really effective police
action except at the expense of other broad purposes of Japanese occupa-
tion.
It is not exaggeration to say that the long term advantages to
Japan of abiding by the short term restrictive provisions of the Promo-
tion and Control of Japanose Economic Recovery will have no appeal
whatever to the ordinary Japanese farmer or laborer, while the Japanese
banker, merchant and industrialist can be expected to pay only ironic
lip service to the hamanity and equity of its broad underlying concept.
In arguing their week by week and month by month problems, Japan's
entrepreneurs will say, with considerable force and persuasiveness,
that increased production cannot be accomplished without inducements
-3

=== Page 206 === (confidence 0.99)
to labor of a sort requiring inereased consumption. In its ease by
case problems, the Japanese Government would be helpless to answer
these arguments except by use of general police authority. And the
exercise of such police authority in peacetime could produce only
imperfect, if any results at all. It is improbable that Scap could
acoomplish, even with the best will and the most admirable plans, what
the Japanese Government itself has failed and would fail to accomplish.
Further, even if consumption curtailmont, imposed by either the Japan-
ese Government or by the occupation authorities, were suceeseful, a
necessary by-product of success would be to help stifle and suppress,
according to plan, those "unplanned" private incentives and motivations
and that real private responsibility which are economic elements inber-
ent in the growth of genuine democratic tendencies in Japan.
C. External Controls Over an Independent Japan
A start is to be mde on the drafting of a Japanese peace
treaty in the near future. Some of those who have favored an early
peace treaty feel that a withdrawal of occupation authority will induce
the Japanese themselves to assume more responsibly and effectively the
running of their own government and economy than has been the case so
long as they could rely upon the protective paternalism of General
MacArthur. Although they may not be optimistic over persistence of
processes of "democratisation" in Japan after withdrawal of the occupy-
ing authorities, they will desire, nevertheless, that kind of peace
treaty which would not positively interfere with sincere indigenous
attempts on the part of the Japanese to put in practice the first
lessons in decentralisation, democracy and individualism which the
occupation authorities have attempted to teach.
Janinese Good Faith May Entail Totalitarian Mothode
Planned production requires strong central government. Even
more so does a program of consumption curtailment. In the light of
history, it is hard to imagine such a central government, if strong
or effective, abiding by middle of the road democratic prooedures in
the accomplishment of its objectives, or failing to tell the people
that their burden was imposed from outside. In short, such a govern-
ment would probably have strong right wing or left wing totalitarian
tendencies. Extremist totalitarian practices would be justified by
the Japanese on the grounds of their necessity if reparations obliga-
tions are to be fulfilled. To answer that argument, the U.S. Govern-
ment and possibly public opinion around the world might well react as
they did, after the mar of 1914-18, by reviewing the problem and con-
sidering either the desirability of terminating Japan's reparations
payments or by pouring in sufficient financial resources to enable
the Japanese to have that economic margin consistent with continued
enjoyment of democratic political practices.
Temptations of Evasion
Far more likely to occur, however, would be a development in

=== Page 207 === (confidence 0.99)
in whish the Japanese captains of industry and commerce would simply
refuse to make good on "reparations" obligations out of current
production, just as soon as the visible authority of the Allied powers
had been removed from the scene. Such a refusal could be coped with
only by inter-Allied intervention, direct or indirect. Allied inter-
vention, after withdraal had once been accomplished, would be an
operation which most countries, the U.S. possibly more than others,
would likely be reluctant to undertake. However, if the Soviets offered
to undertake punitive intervention alone, the U.s. Government might well
find itself in a position of having to support those guiding elements in
Jepan, which would be known to have violated their international oblige-
tions. The development of such a situation could have, five to ten
years hence, obviously undesirable implications.
4. Merits of Cranking Up Even if No Reparations Result
If the above logic can be accepted, it is obvious that the
program of Promotion and Control of Japanese Economic Recovery is likely
to be just and only that and neither, in actuality, a program for re-
paying occupation costs or for increasing the volume or value of repara-
tions to be paid to our Far Eastern Allies. Considered in that light,
the program still has very great merit. Economic rebabilitation in Asia
is going to be accomplished primarily by prompt and maximum increase of
actual industrial and agricultural production and by resumption of normal
current commercial operations. Normal economic revival, not only in
Japan but in all other Far Eastern countries, will far exceed in import-
ance the part which reparations, either in the form of capitel removals
or allocation of Japanese export surpluses, can play. Prospects for
speedy and effective enlargement of productivity are better in Japan
than anywbere else in Asia. A productive Japen contributes to the
wealth of Asia in the short run and can, in the long run, contribute
to economic stability in the Far East as a whole. These economic
certainties and probabilities, however, should not be permitted to
obscure certain political considerationa involved in exercise of U.S.
initiative in deliberateycranking up the Japanese economy. Some of
these political considerations may be of an irrational, emotional, and
even hysterical character, but are not for those reasons any less real.
5. Allied Prejudices and Dangers of U.S. Sponsorship
The State Department's policy on the Promotion and Control of
Japanese Economic Recovery, while sound in concept and eminently en-
lightened in purpose, could be regarded by our Allies in Asia as a
method for asserting a new and novel form of paternalistic "American
colonialism." The proposed cranking up calls for trilateral arrange-
ments wherein Japan immediately benefits by revival of its economy;
wherein the U.S. subsequently benefits from repayment of its costs of
occupation; and wherein all other countries are told to expect ulti-
mate benefits from current reparations, meanwhile participating in

regional interrelationships which will have the effect of putting Japem
on a healthy economie footing before any other Far Eastern eountry
(or for that matter, most European countries) find themselves im a
similar position. In composing this pattern of arrangements, insuf-
ficient cohsideration bas been given, I believe, to csrtain politieal
sentiments and desires of our Far Eastern allies, scme of themlegitimate
and some not. Whether or not making Japan the fabrieator of their raw
materials actually delays their own industrialisation, some of them
think that it will. Whether or not present cranking up of Japanese
industry constitutes a security threat in the long ruh, some of them
suspect that it will. Whether or not the program implies or is likely
to imply prolonged U.S. underwriting of the future of the Japanese
economy, some will think it does. Whether or not this program implies
a transfer of American friendship from the people in Asia who fought
on our side during the war, to the people of Japan against whom we
fought, some will think that such a transfer has occurred.
Only Genuine International Sponsorship Ansmers the Preiudiees
These are the prejudices.
What is involved, then, is weighing the kmown benefits of a
sound economic program for Japan as against the unknowm political
dangers of exercising positive U.S. leadership and undertaking con-
crete U.S. responsibility for a project possibly producing both ime-
diate and long term political dissatisfaction and fear among cther Far
Eastern countries. If a positive program calling for the Promotion
and Control of Japanese Economic Recovery could obtain complete Far
Eastern Commission support, the dangers of "dissatisfaction and fear"
would be removed because representatives of the Far Eastern countries
would have shared in the responsibility for launching such a program.
If that program could result spontaneously from purely Japanese enter-
prise exercised within the framework of existing Far Eastern Commission
policies and understandings, any "dissatisfaction and fear" which arose
among our Allies could not be laid at the U.S. door alone. It is only
if the cranking up progran is conceived and subsequently put in motion
by the U.S. Government alone that those dangers will arise.
Those dangers are of an unpredictable character. The Chinese
and Indian Governments may blame the U.S., not the Japanese, if Japan's
exports continue to keep her over many years in a preferred competitive
trading position in the Far Eastapn textile markets. The metropolitan
powers, seeking to develop markets in their dependencies in southeast
Asia and embarrassed by competition with cheap Japanese exports, way
blame the U.S. for having pressured Japanese fabricated exports into

The above argument leads, I believe, to two negative conclusions:

6. Economic Recovery & Valid Obiective
If it be admitted that a positive program for the revival of
an active and productive Japanese economy can contribute to improvement
in the welfare of the peoples of all Asia, as would, I believe, be
admitted by all except the most churlish representatives of the prinei-
pal Far Eastern eountries, then the problem confronting the U.S. is how
to proceed tomards that objective without exposing itself to the dangers
inherent in assuming excessive responsibility for it. The fremework
within which this aim can be accomplished, I think, has been admirably
laid out in SWNCC 52/7, Part II, paragraph 13, the directive to SCAP
which reads:
"You will not assume any responsibility for the economic rebabilita-
tion of Japan or the strengthening of the Japanese economy. You will
make it clear to the Japanese people that: (a) you assume no obligations
to maintain or have maintained any particular standard of living in
Japan and (b) that the standard of living will depend upon the thorough-
ness with which Japan rids itself of all militaristic ambitions, redirects
the use of its hman and natural resources wholly and solely for purposes
of peaceful living, administers adequate economic and financial controls,
and cooperates with the occupying forces and the governments they
represent."

Japan's Need for Creditas Limited Purpoeses
It is, I believe, an elementary economic fact that Japan cannot
survive without some credit resources. Since Japan's surrender, that
credit has come from Congressional appropriations administered by the
War Department for disease and unrest imports. What is contemplated in
the program for Promotion and Control of the Japanese Econcmic Recovery
is the exercise of U.S. authority in creating credit resources in excess
of such appropriations. One principal source is the liquid foreign
exchange proceeds which may be obtained through planned disposal of
stocks in Japan of convertible assets. The assumption is that the use
of these funds, as operating capital, would contribute to the develop-
ment of exports sufficient to balance costs of imports and ultimately
to such surpluses that the U.S. Government would receive compensation
for its occupation costs and other Far Eastern countries receive repara-
tions from current production. That assumption is so open to challenge
that if the primary motive for cranking up is to recover occupation
costs, serious reconsiderat: should be given to seising the convertible
assets themselves and not gambling upon the possibility that they may in
due course duplicate their own or multiply in value. Since, however,
recovery of occupation costs is not the sole or the most important
objective of the cranking up operation, consideration should be given
to limiting use of the contemplated revolving fund, by its terms of
reference, solely to projects of a strictly self-liquidating character.
By do doing,
a. a limited number of essential industrial projects may be
set in motion,and
b. the initial value of the fund could be preserved in a fprm
quickly available to pass into U.S. hands for partial and legitimmte
repayment of its costs of occupation.
The adoption of this limited concept of the immediate and ulti-
mate use of the revolving fund, concurred at all costs by FEC countries,
would
a. eliminate from our thinking the promise (in all likelihood
a fraudulent promise) of reparations from current production as
now conceived,
b. would eliminate grounds for charges against the U.S. of
sponsoring growth of a powerful Japanese colonial bulmrk, and
c. would minimise the risks that available credit resources
in Japan would be poured down a rat hole from which little more
could be recovered than was recovered from Germany after the last
war.
The point properly may be made that the adoption of such a
position does not permit Japanese economic recovery as effectively as

Eastern economic context necessarily had to be a slow, painful, labor-
ious process undertaken on the initiative of the Japanese people them-
selves who would bear, themselves, full responsibility for their failures.
That assumption, in my view, still remains valid. External assistance
might be a stimulating hypodermic, might produce a flush or passing
fever of activity, but the fundamental problems of Japanese accomodation
to the realities of their economic difficulties cannot be understood or

That process was considered in 1945 as being more likely to contribute

which responsibility for Japanese difficulties and failures ms borne
directly or indirectly by the occupying authorities. There is no
reason to believe that it should be considered differently today.
Nevertheless, the policy for Promotion and Control of Japanese Economic
Recovery conflicts with that judgment by implying, if not explicitly
calling for, outside, particularly U.S., assumption of responsibility
for helping, far beyond any limited case by case extension of credit
for specific production projects to bail Japan out of her present

reshuffle, strengthen the existing entrepreneurial class in Japan, in-

the time when total and desperate economic distress would have forced
upon the Japanese the necessity for creating the kind of new leadership

of the Social Democratic party in the political field.

8. It is my understanding that the role of the State Depar

1. Arising out of several conversations which I have had regarding
my memorandum to you of 13 May, I wish to draw to your attention these
further implications of the proposed State Department policy with respect
to the Promotion and Control of Japanese Economic Recovery.
2. It has been pointed out that serious efforts are being made to
reach an early peace settlement with Japan. This makes it likely that
the provisions for such control, by the Japanese Government itself, as
will enable repayment of occupation costs and payment of reparations out
of current output, must be written into the Japanese peace treaty. Sueh

control provisions might very well be in conflict with current War and
